questions.q: In C, what is a constant defined with `#define`, such as `#define N (20)`?
choices: An alias for a literal value (here, the literal 20)
A variable whose value is set once when the program starts
A pointer to a read-only memory location that holds 20
A function that returns 20
questions.explain: A constant is an alias for a C literal value. Wherever `N` appears in the code, it stands for the literal `20`.

questions.q:
What happens with this code?
```c
#define N 20

int main(void) {
  N = 50;
  ...
```
choices: Compilation error: `N` is not an lvalue, so the line is effectively `20 = 50`
`N` becomes 50 for the rest of `main`
`N` becomes 50 everywhere in the program
It compiles, but the assignment has no effect at runtime
questions.explain: Constants are aliases for literal values, not variables, so they are not lvalues and can't be changed at runtime. `N = 50` means `20 = 50`, which is not valid C.

questions.q:
Fill in the blank so that `PI` is a constant that aliases the literal 3.14:
```c
____ PI (3.14)
```
questions.explain: Constants are defined with the syntax `#define const_name (literal_value)`.

choices: The array, the malloc'd block, and the loop all now use 50
Only `array` changes size; the `malloc` call and loop bound must be edited by hand
Nothing changes unless `N` is also reassigned inside `main`
Only the loop bound changes; array sizes stay as they were first written
questions.explain: Every use of a constant refers to its definition. Changing the one `#define` line and recompiling updates all the code that uses it.

questions.q: Which are reasons to use a constant `PI` instead of writing `3.14` directly throughout a program?
choices: In an expression, `PI` carries more meaning than `3.14`, so the code is more readable
To change the value everywhere, you edit one definition and recompile
The program can update `PI` while it runs, like a variable
You can take its address with `&PI` and pass it to a function
questions.explain: Constants make code more readable and easier to modify. They are aliases for literal values, not lvalues, so they can't be changed at runtime and have no address to take.

questions.q:
```c
#define ROWS (4)
#define COLS (3)

int grid[ROWS * COLS];
```
How many `int` elements does `grid` hold?
questions.explain: `ROWS * COLS` stands for `(4) * (3)`, which is 12.

questions.q: When a `switch` statement runs and no `case` value matches the expression, what happens?
choices: If there is a `default` label, its statements run; otherwise no statements in the switch body run
The statements under the first `case` run
The statements under the last `case` run
The program stops with a runtime error
questions.explain: The expression is evaluated and then compared against the case values. If nothing matches, execution starts at `default` if one exists. Otherwise the whole switch body is skipped.
`case 8` matches, so `new_num = 8 - 1 = 7`. Then `break` exits the switch.
Execution starts at `case 8` and sets `new_num` to 7. Because there's no `break`, it falls through into `case 9`, sets `new_num = 8 + 2 = 10`, and then reaches that case's `break`.
Execution starts at the matching `case 2` (count = 10). With no `break`, it continues into `case 3` (count = 110). The `break` there exits the switch, so `case 4` never runs.

questions.q: What does a `break` statement do when it is reached inside a `switch` body?
choices: Stops executing the switch body and continues with the next statement after the whole switch block
Skips ahead to the next `case` label
Jumps to the `default` label
Returns from the enclosing function
questions.explain: `break` stops all remaining statements in the switch body. Execution continues with the first statement after the switch.

questions.q: A `switch` statement can replace any chain of `if`-`else if` statements.
questions.explain: `switch` can replace some `if`-`else if` chains, but not all of them. It only tests one expression for equality against fixed case values, so a chain like `if (x > 10) ... else if (y < 0) ...` can't be written as a switch.

questions.q: Assume `num` is an `int` variable and `WED` is a constant in an enumerated type. Which are valid `case` labels?
choices: `case 7:`
`case WED:`
`case num:`
`case num > 5:`
questions.explain: A case value must be a literal value. An enum constant like `WED` is an alias for an int literal, so it is allowed. A variable, or an expression that uses one, can't be a case label. The switch expression is only compared for equality with each case's value.

choices: `Orchestra practice today` followed by `PSYCH 101 and CS 231 today`
Only `Orchestra practice today`
`Orchestra practice today`, `PSYCH 101 and CS 231 today`, and `Math 311 and HIST 140 today`
`Error: 6 is not a valid day`
questions.explain: `case FRI` has no `break`, so after its `printf` runs, execution falls through into the statements shared by `MON` and `WED`. It stops at the `break` there.

questions.q:
```c
enum color { RED, GREEN, BLUE };
```
What integer value does `BLUE` have?
questions.explain: By default the first constant is 0 and each one after it is one more: RED=0, GREEN=1, BLUE=2.
`= 5` starts the sequence at 5. The constants after it continue in order: MEDIUM=6, HIGH=7.
Enum constants are aliases for int values, so the value prints as an integer, not as its name. Here it prints `Today is 2`.

questions.q: Compared with defining the same values as separate `#define` constants, which are advantages of an enumerated type?
choices: It groups a set of related integer constants together
It is a type, so variables and parameters can be declared with it
Values are assigned automatically in sequence, so you don't have to write each one
Constants can be added or removed without manually renumbering the others
`printf` can print an enum value as its constant's name
Its constants can hold floating-point values such as 3.14
questions.explain: An enum groups related integer constants, defines a type, assigns values in sequence implicitly, and lets you add or remove constants easily. Its values are ints, so they print as numbers and can't be floating-point values.

questions.q:
A program has:
```c
enum days_of_week { MON, TUES, WED, THURS, FRI };
```
The programmer adds `SUN` before `MON` and `SAT` after `FRI`, without assigning any explicit values. What is the value of `FRI` now?
questions.explain: Values are assigned in order starting at 0: SUN=0, MON=1, TUES=2, WED=3, THURS=4, FRI=5, SAT=6. The other constants are renumbered automatically.

questions.q: Given `enum days_of_week { MON, TUES, WED, THURS, FRI };` and no typedef, which line correctly declares a variable `day` of this type?
choices: `enum days_of_week day;`
`days_of_week day;`
`enum day = days_of_week;`
`day enum days_of_week;`
questions.explain: The type name is `enum type_name`, so the declaration is `enum days_of_week day;`. Without a typedef, `days_of_week` on its own is not a type name.

choices: `Math 311 and HIST 140 today`
`PSYCH 101 and CS 231 today`
`Do weekly pre-readings`
`Error: 3 is not a valid day`
questions.explain: With `SUN = 1`, the values continue in sequence: MON=2, TUES=3. So 3 matches `case TUES`, which shares its statements with `THURS`.

questions.q: Which line makes `ull` an alias for the type `unsigned long long`?
choices: `typedef unsigned long long ull;`
`typedef ull unsigned long long;`
`typedef ull = unsigned long long;`
`typedef ull (unsigned long long);`
questions.explain: The format is `typedef existing_type_name new_type_alias_name;`. The existing type comes first and the new alias comes last.

questions.q: Which C keyword defines a new name that is an alias for an existing type?
questions.explain: `typedef` creates a type alias. Once it is defined, you can declare variables using the alias.

choices: Both the struct type `struct point` and the alias `point` for it
Only the alias `point`; `struct point` can't be used
Only `struct point`; the trailing `point` declares a variable named `point`
A variable named `point` with an unnamed struct type
questions.explain: When `typedef` comes before a struct definition, the name after the closing `}` becomes a type alias, not a variable. This defines `struct point` and the alias `point` at the same time.

choices: `struct point p1;`
`point p2;`
`point struct p3;`
`enum point p4;`
questions.explain: The combined definition creates both `struct point` and its alias `point`, so you can declare variables with either name. The other two choices are not valid type names.
`classYr` is an alias for `enum class_year`. With FIRST=1, the values are SECOND=2, JUNIOR=3, SENIOR=4, and they print as integers.

questions.q: What is `typedef` commonly used for?
choices: Giving types shorter, more readable names, often for structs and enumerated types
Making a variable read-only after it is initialized
Allocating memory for a struct
Defining a group of related integer constants
questions.explain: `typedef` defines an alias for an existing type. It is often used to give struct and enum types shorter names. Grouping related integer constants is what `enum` does.

questions.q: `typedef` can only create aliases for struct types.
questions.explain: `typedef` works with any existing type. For example, `typedef enum class_year classYr;` and `typedef unsigned long long ull;` are both valid.
Putting `typedef` before the struct definition and the alias name after the closing `}` is equivalent to defining the struct and then writing the typedef as a separate line.
